title: Data Types and Type Behaviour Across DBMS Products
learningObjectives: Describe SQLite's dynamic typing and type-affinity model.
Explain why server DBMS data types may enforce different ranges and precision.
Choose data types deliberately for money, dates, booleans and identifiers.
Use constraints and application validation to protect required value rules.

understand.concept: Database products represent and enforce data types differently. SQLite uses dynamic typing with type affinity, while server DBMS products commonly enforce more rigid column types and offer product-specific precision, date/time and boolean types.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing the correct type affects storage, arithmetic precision, sorting, validation and application interoperability.
understand.analogy: SQL portability is like translating a precise instruction into several product dialects: the intent stays the same, but the exact words and rules can differ.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model type systems, function return types, time-zone rules, optimizer behaviour or transaction semantics.

explain.narrative:
## SQLite type affinity
SQLite associates storage classes with values and applies type affinity based on declared column types. INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and NUMERIC are the main storage classes. A declared type name influences affinity but does not behave exactly like a rigid server-side type system.

## Server DBMS differences
PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server provide richer native types and different rules for DECIMAL precision, timestamps, time zones, booleans, JSON and binary values. The same type name can have different ranges or semantics.

## Practical design
Use exact numeric types for money in server databases, define precision and scale deliberately, store dates consistently, and validate application input. For SQLite, understand how values are stored and use constraints where the application requires stronger validation.

### Type systems differ
SQLite uses dynamic typing and column affinity; PostgreSQL and SQL Server use comparatively rigid native types; MySQL has its own conversion and strict-mode rules. The same declared type name can have different ranges, precision, collation and coercion behaviour.

### Exact numeric and temporal design
For money, use an exact DECIMAL/NUMERIC type with defined precision and scale where the DBMS enforces it, or integer minor units. For time values, choose whether the column represents a calendar date, local wall time or a UTC instant, then use the target engine's appropriate type and conversion rules.

examples.title: Create columns with different SQLite affinities
examples.code: CREATE TABLE dialect16_types (integer_value INTEGER, real_value REAL, text_value TEXT, blob_value BLOB, numeric_value NUMERIC);
examples.explanation: Creates columns with SQLite type affinities. SQLite derives affinity from declared type names and stores values using storage classes; it does not enforce a rigid per-column type system in the same way as PostgreSQL or SQL Server.

examples.title: Insert values into typed columns
examples.explanation: Inserts an integer, real number, text string, two-byte blob and decimal-looking value. The X'4142' literal is SQLite's hexadecimal blob notation; numeric_value is stored as REAL under NUMERIC affinity for this value.

examples.title: Inspect SQLite storage classes
examples.code: SELECT typeof(integer_value), typeof(real_value), typeof(text_value), typeof(blob_value), typeof(numeric_value) FROM dialect16_types;
examples.explanation: Calls typeof() for each column to inspect the actual SQLite storage class of the inserted value. The result shows integer, real, text, blob and real respectively, rather than merely echoing the declared type names.

examples.title: Use a CHECK constraint to validate a numeric range
examples.code: CREATE TABLE dialect16_scores (score INTEGER CHECK (score BETWEEN 0 AND 100));
examples.explanation: Creates a score table with a CHECK range. CHECK evaluates the row expression during writes, but SQL CHECK constraints generally do not reject NULL unless the expression evaluates to false; use NOT NULL as well if a score is required.

examples.title: Verify a stored decimal-like value
examples.explanation: Reads the decimal-looking value and its storage class. The result confirms 12.75 is stored as a floating-point REAL value in this fixture, which is why binary floating-point should not be used as an unexamined financial representation.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and compare declared column types with the storage classes returned by typeof().
practise.independentTask: Design a customer and payment schema. Identify which types are portable and which need DBMS-specific choices for money, date/time and boolean values.
hints: SQLite has INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and NUMERIC storage classes.
A declared type influences affinity but does not guarantee rigid storage.
Server DBMS products often enforce precision and type ranges more strictly.
Use CHECK constraints for domain rules when appropriate.
Test numeric precision and date/time behaviour in the target DBMS.
